t: Sons of God or angels of God?
p: The Greek translates 'the angels of God'. The Hebrew has 'the sons of God'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex, AD 1008); Targum; Vulgate (filii Dei)
readings.en: the sons of God
readings.plain: the sons of God

readings.en: the angels of God
readings.plain: the angels of God

why: The Greek is a translation, not a different Hebrew text: the translator explained the phrase as angels, as the Greek also does at Genesis 6:2 in some manuscripts and Deuteronomy 32:8. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew phrase and explains it in a note.
b: Both readings mean the same beings, members of God's heavenly court. The Hebrew phrase keeps the picture of a royal council of divine beings (see the divine-council topic and Psalm 82; Psalm 89:6–7); the Greek reading reflects the way Jews of the 200s and 100s BC spoke of them, as angels. The same choice returns at 38:7.

a: The LORD gave, and the LORD took.
p: The Old Greek adds 'As it seemed good to the Lord, so it has happened' before the blessing.

readings.en: The LORD gave and the LORD took
readings.plain: The LORD gave, and the LORD took.

readings.orig: ὁ κύριος ἔδωκεν, ὁ κύριος ἀφείλατο· ὡς τῷ κυρίῳ ἔδοξεν, οὕτως καὶ ἐγένετο
readings.en: The Lord gave, the Lord took away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it also happened
readings.plain: The LORD gave, and the LORD took. As it seemed good to the Lord, so it has happened.

why: The added line is found only in the Greek and in translations made from it. It reads like an explanation that stresses God's will, and the shorter Hebrew is followed by almost all translations.

a: His wife said to him, "Still holding on to your integrity? Curse God, and die."
t: The Greek speech of Job's wife
p: In the Old Greek, Job's wife speaks a long lament for her children and her own suffering before telling him to speak against the Lord.

readings.orig: וַתֹּאמֶר לוֹ אִשְׁתּוֹ עֹדְךָ מַחֲזִיק בְּתֻמָּתֶךָ בָּרֵךְ אֱלֹהִים וָמֻת
readings.en: And his wife said to him, Are you still holding fast your integrity? Bless (curse) God and die
readings.plain: His wife said to him, "Still holding on to your integrity? Curse God, and die."

readings.w: Old Greek (Rahlfs 2:9 with 2:9a–e; checked at blueletterbible.org; English after NETS)
readings.orig: χρόνου δὲ πολλοῦ προβεβηκότος εἶπεν αὐτῷ ἡ γυνὴ αὐτοῦ ... ἀλλὰ εἰπόν τι ῥῆμα εἰς κύριον καὶ τελεύτα
readings.en: After much time had passed, his wife said to him ... But say some word against the Lord and die
readings.plain: After a long time had passed, his wife said to him, "How long will you hold out, saying, 'Look, I will wait a little longer, hoping to be rescued'? Look, the memory of you has vanished from the earth: our sons and daughters, the birth pains and labors of my womb, whom I wore myself out raising for nothing. And you sit in the rot of worms, spending the nights out in the open, while I wander about as a servant, from place to place and house to house, waiting for the sun to go down so that I can rest from the labors and pains that grip me now. Just say some word against the Lord, and die."

why: The long speech is found only in the Greek and in translations made from it; no Hebrew manuscript has it, and no Qumran manuscript preserves this verse. It reads as an expansion that gives the wife a voice and a grief of her own. The Plain English Translation follows the Hebrew. The Greek speech is rendered here from Rahlfs' text in this site's own words.
b: The Greek wife is far more sympathetic than the Hebrew one: she has watched her children die, she has become a day laborer to feed her husband, and her final words are softened from "curse God" to "say some word against the Lord." The Testament of Job expands her story further, names her Sitis, and has her sell her hair to Satan for bread. Many scholars think the Greek translator, or the tradition he followed, wanted to explain why a long time passed (the Hebrew of 7:3 speaks of months) and to answer readers who were shocked by her words. Note that the Greek, like the Hebrew of 1:11 and 2:5, avoids writing "curse God" outright.

a: those who are ready to wake Leviathan.
t: Leviathan or the great sea monster
p: The Greek reads 'the one who is about to subdue the great sea monster'.

readings.en: those ready to rouse Leviathan
readings.plain: those who are ready to wake Leviathan.

readings.orig: ὁ μέλλων τὸ μέγα κῆτος χειρώσασθαι
readings.en: the one who is about to subdue the great sea monster
readings.plain: the one who is about to subdue the great sea monster.

why: The Greek translator explained Leviathan as the great sea monster and made the curser the one who will master it, perhaps thinking of God or a hero. The Hebrew, harder and stranger, is followed by almost all translations. The modern proposal to read 'Sea' (yam) for 'day' (yom) in the first line is a conjecture with no manuscript support; see the note.
b: The small Aramaic translation from Qumran Cave 4 (4QtgJob, 4Q157) preserves broken pieces of 3:5–9. It was not checked directly by this writer, and the fragments are too damaged to settle the readings of 3:5 or 3:8; see Milik's edition in DJD 6.

a: and then, in a moment, I cursed his homestead.
p: The Greek says the fools' home 'was eaten up' at once, where the Hebrew has 'I cursed'.

readings.en: and I cursed his dwelling suddenly
readings.plain: and then, in a moment, I cursed his homestead.

readings.orig: ἀλλ᾽ εὐθέως ἐβρώθη αὐτῶν ἡ δίαιτα
readings.en: but suddenly their way of life was eaten up
readings.plain: but suddenly their home was eaten up.

why: The Hebrew is the harder reading, and the Greek may be the translator's way around a speaker cursing someone. Many modern scholars emend the Hebrew to 'it was cursed' or 'it rotted'; the Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and gives the options in a note.
b: The Cave 4 Aramaic Targum (4QtgJob, 4Q157) covers parts of 4:16–5:4 and so may preserve something of this line. It was not checked directly by this writer; the fragment is very broken, and its reading here is not used.

a: and a snare gapes open for their wealth.
p: The Hebrew 'snare' is often changed to 'the thirsty', as the Vulgate read it.

readings.en: and a snare pants (gapes) for their wealth
readings.plain: and a snare gapes open for their wealth.

readings.w: Vulgate (sitientes, 'the thirsty'); many modern versions, reading tsme'im
readings.en: and the thirsty pant for their wealth
readings.plain: and the thirsty pant after their wealth.

readings.en: may their strength be drained out
readings.plain: and may their strength be drained away.

why: The Masoretic word tsammim, 'snare' (as in 18:9), makes sense: the trap is open for the fool's goods. 'The thirsty' gives a neater pair with 'the hungry' in the first line, and many translators prefer it, but it needs a change of the Hebrew. The KJV's 'the robber' is another attempt to explain tsammim.

a: That is what you have turned into now.
p: The written Hebrew says 'you have become nothing'; the margin reads 'you have become like it' (the dry wadi).

readings.w: Qere (the Masoretes' reading in the margin), Leningrad Codex
readings.en: for now you have become (like) it
readings.plain: That is what you have turned into now.

readings.w: Ketiv (the written consonants); followed by the KJV and many modern versions
readings.en: for now you have become nothing
readings.plain: Now you have become nothing.

readings.orig: ἀτὰρ δὲ καὶ ὑμεῖς ἐπέβητέ μοι ἀνελεημόνως
readings.en: but you too have come upon me without mercy
readings.plain: Now you too have come at me without mercy.

why: The Qere links the friends to the dry stream of 6:15–20, which fits the passage. The Ketiv, 'nothing', is also good Hebrew and is followed by many translations. The Greek paraphrases.

a: so that I am a burden to myself?
p: The Hebrew says 'a burden to myself'. The Greek and an old scribal tradition say 'a burden to you'.

readings.w: Masoretic Text (Leningrad Codex); Vulgate (mihimet ipsi); KJV
readings.en: and I have become a burden to myself
readings.plain: so that I am a burden to myself?

readings.w: Old Greek (Rahlfs; checked at blueletterbible.org); the rabbinic lists of 'corrections of the scribes' (tiqqune soferim); many modern versions
readings.en: and I am a burden on you
readings.plain: so that I am a burden to you?

why: Jewish tradition counts this verse among the eighteen 'corrections of the scribes', places where scribes are said to have changed an expression that seemed irreverent toward God, here 'to you' into 'to me'. The Greek supports 'to you', and many translators follow it. But the lists of corrections are late and not always reliable, and the Hebrew makes good sense: God's attack has made Job's own life unbearable. The Plain English Translation keeps the Hebrew and gives the other reading here.
b: If 'to you' is original, Job's question is daring: why would God make a mere human a burden to himself, God? That fits Job's irony in 7:17–21, where God treats a breath of a man as a great threat. If 'to myself' is original, the line turns inward: God has made Job's existence a weight he cannot carry. Both readings are in the major translations.

a: Through all this Job did not sin with his lips.
p: The Greek adds 'before God' at the end of the verse.

readings.en: Job did not sin with his lips
readings.plain: Through all this Job did not sin with his lips.

readings.en: Job did not sin with his lips before God
readings.plain: Through all this Job did not sin with his lips before God.

why: A small Greek plus that makes the verse a judgment made in God's sight; the Hebrew is shorter and followed by translations generally.
